strings.title: Gemini 4 Neon Use Cases
strings.scope: Explore Gemini 4 Neon through public workflows, visual prototypes, integrations, and evaluations. Each case links to its source and describes the model's role and the reported result.
strings.step_1: Choose a case from the menu and open its original source.
strings.step_2: Check the model role, tool, settings and outcome that the source reports.
strings.step_3: Compare cases with matching tasks and settings. Treat creator-reported times and costs as observations from those runs.
strings.carbon: Gemini 4 Carbon Guide and Use Cases
strings.thanks: Thanks to the creators and evaluators who shared their work.
strings.corrections: Media and third-party work remain with their respective rights holders. Please open an issue if a source, credit, or media item needs correction.
strings.overview_sentence: **{cases} Gemini 4 Neon cases** with {visuals} source visuals.
strings.evidence_note: Each case links to its source. Treat reported timings, costs, and benchmarks as observations from the stated test conditions.

case-1.title: Observe instability during unattended runs
case-1.takeaway: The tester reports launch-day instability when running Neon headlessly and says Opus 5.5 monitored the run.
case-1.notes: The screenshots document that environment. The report does not attribute the root cause.
case-1.action: Track retries and completion in unattended runs, and keep a separate record of the supervising model.

case-2.title: Build a simulated logic-gate demo
case-2.takeaway: The author shows an interactive electronics demo that goes from simulated logic gates and circuit boards to a retro terminal display.
case-2.notes: The series reports one prompt per demo without refinement. The recording shows the interface and simulation behavior.
case-2.action: Check what the simulation shows at the chip, circuit board and display levels.

case-3.title: Design a Bluetooth toothbrush in tscircuit
case-3.takeaway: A tscircuit maintainer compared Neon High, Opus 5.5 High and Sol 6.2 High on a Bluetooth electric toothbrush.
case-3.notes: The maintainer preferred Neon's visual result but reported incomplete routing and poor footprint choices.
case-3.action: Review routing and footprint selection independently of the rendered enclosure.

case-4.title: Relay a Muse side conversation to Neon
case-4.takeaway: The author built a Muse side chat that passes requests and replies through to Neon.
case-4.notes: The posted Japanese instruction configures the Muse relay. It is an instruction to Muse and does not establish a direct prompt sent to Neon.
case-4.action: Check which replies come from Neon before relying on the Muse relay.

case-5.title: Use Neon for copy in a three-model T3 Code workflow
case-5.takeaway: The developer gives Neon the copywriting role within a multi-model T3 Code workflow.
case-5.notes: The developer assigns implementation to Fable and playtesting to GPT-6.2 Astra. The T3 Code screenshot shows a creature-raising game with copywriters in the active workflow.
case-5.action: Assign one model to copywriting and check its handoff to implementation and playtesting.

case-6.title: Rework a Spotify recommendation MCP
case-6.takeaway: The creator used Neon to revise a Spotify recommendation MCP originally built with Argon.
case-6.notes: The creator reported bug fixes and an unrequested taste-based recommendation model. The post does not provide recommendation accuracy.
case-6.action: Review recommendation changes and test whether unrequested features improve the result.

case-7.title: Draw an SVG side view of a car
case-7.takeaway: The creator used Neon high in AI Studio to create a BMW M4 CS side-view SVG.
case-7.notes: The artifact is attached to the post. No complete prompt is quoted.
case-7.action: Check proportion and silhouette when comparing code-rendered side views.

case-8.title: Run an SVG test series
case-8.takeaway: The tester shared three outputs in a Neon SVG test series.
case-8.notes: The results are presented together and counted as one test series.
case-8.action: Review several outputs before judging consistency across SVG tasks.

case-9.title: Animate a pelican in Three.js
case-9.takeaway: The tester attributes a Three.js pelican-on-a-bicycle output to Neon.
case-9.notes: The creator provides a recording but no timing or reasoning setting.
case-9.action: Check the cycling motion and scene rendering as separate parts of the animation.

case-10.title: Draw an SVG portrait at xhigh
case-10.takeaway: The tester shares a portrait of Ana de Armas attributed to Neon xhigh.
case-10.notes: The source gives the subject and effort setting without the exact prompt.
case-10.action: Assess likeness and SVG editability separately in a portrait test.

case-11.title: Animate a cycling pelican at medium effort
case-11.takeaway: The author used Neon at medium effort to produce a pelican cycling demo and posted the video.
case-11.notes: The clip documents this creator's separate run of a common test task.
case-11.action: Use a fixed animation task to compare results at different reasoning settings.

case-12.title: Compare two voxel garden scenes
case-12.takeaway: The author posted a voxel garden from Neon xhigh alongside a GPT-6.2 Sol xhigh result.
case-12.notes: The source identifies the first image as Neon and reports USD 1.01 versus USD 0.19 for Sol. The post does not specify whether the prompts and tools matched.
case-12.action: Check similar-looking outputs against total run cost and the settings each source discloses.

case-13.title: Generate a Three.js and GLSL scene
case-13.takeaway: The creator shares a Three.js and GLSL output from Neon and reports a run of two minutes and 40 seconds.
case-13.notes: The main post points to the replies for the instruction without quoting it.
case-13.action: Separate shader behavior, scene geometry, and generation time in a graphics test.

case-14.title: Create paintings entirely in code
case-14.takeaway: The creator reports using early-access Neon to write code that renders paintings.
case-14.notes: The source provides a set of results from the same series. It does not supply each exact prompt.
case-14.action: Open the rendered examples to see how code can produce a coherent visual series.

case-15.title: Compare pelican cycling animations
case-15.takeaway: The tester compared a pelican animation across Neon, Hydrogen, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol.
case-15.notes: The author reports a three-minute Neon run and preferred its appearance. The recorded Sol-only follow-up belongs to the same test.
case-15.action: Compare the reported runtime with the movement and scene details in the same video.

case-16.title: Compare Three.js cycling animations across three models
case-16.takeaway: The tester published a Three.js cycling comparison of Neon, Opus 5.5 and Carbon.
case-16.notes: The author preferred Neon over Opus and judged it close to Carbon. This is the author's visual assessment.
case-16.action: Use the labeled clips to compare motion, lighting, and scene composition.

case-17.title: Render a tall ship on the ocean
case-17.takeaway: The tester shared an ocean sailing scene attributed to Neon xhigh.
case-17.notes: The video shows an animated sailing ship. The source does not supply a specific workflow or timing.
case-17.action: Inspect whether wave animation and ship rendering remain coherent throughout the clip.

case-18.title: Generate a voxel pagoda
case-18.takeaway: The tester posts a voxel pagoda generated at Neon xhigh.
case-18.notes: The post includes the rendered result and the author's design reaction.
case-18.action: Use the voxel scene to assess layering, silhouette, and composition.

case-19.title: Draw a frustrated pelican on a bicycle
case-19.takeaway: The creator used Neon high in AI Studio to draw an SVG of a frustrated pelican riding a bicycle.
case-19.notes: The post shows the result and identifies the effort setting.
case-19.action: Check whether the character expression and bicycle motion both read clearly.

case-20.title: Compare gamepad drawings with GPT-6.2 Sol
case-20.takeaway: The tester used the same prompt at each model's highest available reasoning and judged the outputs similar.
case-20.notes: The author reported 20 minutes and about USD 1.60 for Neon versus nine minutes and about USD 0.53 for Sol.
case-20.action: Compare render quality and time and cost separately for the two gamepad outputs.

case-21.title: Generate a 3D seaplane
case-21.takeaway: The tester used Neon xhigh to build a 3D seaplane and shared a video.
case-21.notes: The creator describes the build as fast and the interface as cleaner, without giving a wall-clock measurement.
case-21.action: Review the seaplane and water interaction before judging the prototype as a whole.

case-22.title: Draw a 2D horse
case-22.takeaway: The creator used Neon to produce a two-dimensional horse and posted the output.
case-22.notes: The creator preferred it to their prior Gemini results. The post does not provide matching settings.
case-22.action: Treat the horse clip as a visual example and keep cross-model settings in mind.

case-23.title: Test a rainy convenience-store scene
case-23.takeaway: The tester used the same prompt for Neon and GPT-6.2 Sol and posted the comparison.
case-23.notes: The author preferred the Sol visual output while reporting faster, cheaper completion for Neon in this run.
case-23.action: Use the matched scene to assess how presentation changes with shorter generation time.

case-24.title: Animate a robotic quadruped from one image
case-24.takeaway: The developer gave Neon a single reference image and asked for a 3D model.
case-24.notes: The developer reports a Three.js WebGPU demonstration with four-leg inverse kinematics and walk, trot and gallop animations.
case-24.action: Check gait and movement separately from how closely the scene follows the reference.

case-25.title: Animate Keats in vanilla JavaScript
case-25.takeaway: A Google team member credits GeokenAI and Neon for a vanilla JavaScript animation of Keats's To Autumn.
case-25.notes: The post describes a 12 fps painterly 3D animation with no libraries. The sharing account is distinct from the credited creator.
case-25.action: Compare animation and brushwork when using code to interpret a literary source.

case-26.title: Create a Triceratops demo
case-26.takeaway: The creator attributes the Triceratops demonstration to Neon.
case-26.notes: The video shows the artifact. The post does not specify the input format or generation steps.
case-26.action: Inspect the reconstruction sequence as well as the final visual.

case-27.title: Compare 3D gear train renderings
case-27.takeaway: The tester shows gear mechanism renders for Neon, Carbon, Astra and Sol across the labeled reasoning levels.
case-27.notes: The author favored Neon. The clip documents one visual comparison and does not establish the general cost claim.
case-27.action: Use the labeled settings and output geometry to compare all four gear-train renders.

case-28.title: Build ten interactive effects in a single HTML file
case-28.takeaway: A Google team member reports using Neon to create ten interactive 3D effects in one 27 KB HTML file.
case-28.notes: The demo includes shaders, water and lighting. The variations are grouped as one published project.
case-28.action: Check whether the effects stay responsive and readable within a small HTML payload.

case-29.title: Build a Blender lab bench with Antigravity Swarm
case-29.takeaway: Google demonstrated Neon using Antigravity Swarm and Blender to produce a lab-bench scene themed around the Gemini 4 family.
case-29.notes: The clip is a provider demo of the integrated workflow.
case-29.action: Trace which work Swarm coordinates and which operations Blender performs.

case-30.title: Compare architectural illustrations with Opus 5.5
case-30.takeaway: The tester compared the models using the same prompt at their highest available reasoning.
case-30.notes: The author reported about 20 minutes and USD 3.50 for Neon and 18 minutes and USD 7.20 for Opus, preferring the Opus output.
case-30.action: Set the same visual task and compare the output quality, run time, and cost independently.

case-31.title: Visualize Voyager 1's flight
case-31.takeaway: The author shows a 3D Voyager 1 sequence that moves from launch to a Jupiter encounter and a close-up of the spacecraft.
case-31.notes: The author describes this as one unrefined prompt in the series. No trajectory validation is reported.
case-31.action: Review the transitions between the launch, flyby and close-up when judging the sequence.

case-32.title: Build a 3D planetarium
case-32.takeaway: The author shows a 3D planetarium moving between planets and a constellation view.
case-32.notes: The recording shows examples including Earth and Saturn. The one-prompt series does not establish astronomical precision.
case-32.action: Check whether the planet and constellation views work together as a simple educational demo.

case-33.title: Visualize Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2
case-33.takeaway: The author shows a 3D visualization of Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2 with its gear assemblies and a numerical display.
case-33.notes: The recording moves between close-ups of the moving mechanism and a view of the complete machine.
case-33.action: Look at the gear motion, numerical display and full-machine view when reviewing the visualization.

case-34.title: Visualize the Antikythera mechanism
case-34.takeaway: The author shows a 3D Antikythera mechanism demo that switches between the recovered object, reconstructed gears and a dial.
case-34.notes: The recording shows a display of the assembly and details of the moving mechanism.
case-34.action: Compare the recovered fragment view, gear reconstruction and dial readout in the same demo.

case-35.title: Prototype a visual wind tunnel
case-35.takeaway: The author shows a 3D wind-tunnel demo with visible airflow streamlines around different shapes.
case-35.notes: The video includes an aircraft and other test shapes. It gives no independent accuracy check for the simulation.
case-35.action: Compare how the streamlines change between test shapes before using the visualization as a teaching example.

case-36.title: Create a King's College Chapel cutaway
case-36.takeaway: The author shows a 3D cutaway of King's College Chapel that switches between the exterior and interior.
case-36.notes: The scene uses different views to show the nave, windows and the building's cross-section.
case-36.action: Compare the exterior, nave and cutaway to see how each view explains the building.

case-37.title: Render a river viaduct and its surroundings
case-37.takeaway: The author shows a 3D river valley with a multi-arch viaduct, a train and several render views.
case-37.notes: The recording switches between near and distant camera angles and includes a wireframe-like view.
case-37.action: Use the near, far and wireframe views to assess both the bridge and its surrounding scene.

case-38.title: Build a Cambridge-inspired 3D city view
case-38.takeaway: The author shows a city visualization inspired by Cambridge, with aerial and closer views of the modeled blocks.
case-38.notes: The clip shows the river, buildings and scene overlays. The author describes the setting as Cambridge-like.
case-38.action: Check how landmarks and the river remain recognizable as the camera moves through the scene.

case-39.title: Render a neon-themed Earth
case-39.takeaway: The creator used Neon high in Antigravity to render a neon-themed planet.
case-39.notes: The source provides the result and effort setting.
case-39.action: Check whether the visual theme is consistent as the globe rotates.

case-40.title: Iterate a yacht scene
case-40.takeaway: The creator reports that Neon improved a yacht scene and shows the output.
case-40.notes: Firebase deployment was a stated intention at the time of the post.
case-40.action: Review before-and-after artifacts when asking the model to refine a 3D scene.

case-41.title: Make costume materials in a custom VFX tool
case-41.takeaway: The creator used Neon to make costume materials and posted six images of results.
case-41.notes: The creator describes the VFX tooling as their own. The source does not establish an independent performance comparison.
case-41.action: Compare treatments of the same costume form when choosing a material.

case-42.title: Compare voxel Ninjago scenes
case-42.takeaway: The source compares Neon and Fable 5.2 on a voxel recreation.
case-42.notes: The author reports USD 12.93 for Neon and USD 11.19 for Fable and preferred the latter's framing.
case-42.action: Judge visual framing and cost separately in a same-subject voxel comparison.

case-43.title: Create a pelican product motion graphic
case-43.takeaway: The creator credits Neon with a pelican-themed product motion graphic.
case-43.notes: The linked clip shows the output. The post does not describe implementation or an exact prompt.
case-43.action: Look at timing and typography together in a short product animation.

case-44.title: Compare New York City scene prototypes
case-44.takeaway: The tester reports that Neon included the Brooklyn Bridge, Statue of Liberty and a street with taxis.
case-44.notes: The tester preferred some details in the Opus output and reported that running the Neon scene lagged their PC.
case-44.action: Evaluate landmark fidelity and runtime performance separately in a city-scene build.

case-45.title: Run a banana visual test
case-45.takeaway: The tester posts a Neon output for a test titled Banana Test.
case-45.notes: The output is attached to the source. The source does not provide an exact prompt.
case-45.action: Inspect how a simple visual task holds up across details and proportions.

case-46.title: Compare a haunted cathedral on one prompt
case-46.takeaway: The tester gave Neon and GPT-6.2 Sol the same haunted cathedral task.
case-46.notes: The creator reports USD 2.67 for Neon and USD 1.69 for Sol, with no clear visual winner in their assessment.
case-46.action: Use the published prompt to compare the two cathedral renders under the conditions described.

case-47.title: Prototype a phone assembly in Antigravity
case-47.takeaway: The developer used Neon in Antigravity and showed a board of design components and a rendered phone assembly.
case-47.notes: The developer reports early impressions of coding and speed, without timings or a controlled Carbon comparison.
case-47.action: Check component fidelity and final assembly separately when reviewing a design prototype.

case-48.title: Generate an interactive historical sailing ship
case-48.takeaway: The author posted a zero-shot 3D sailing ship demonstration.
case-48.notes: The author reports that the ship and water rendered in distinct layers and describes the output as more realistic than their Sol result.
case-48.action: Inspect the boundaries between the ship and water in the interactive output.

case-49.title: Design a model introduction in JavaScript
case-49.takeaway: The author used Neon to make a motion graphic introducing the model.
case-49.notes: The author says it uses JavaScript without external assets.
case-49.action: Review typography and pacing in the JavaScript motion graphic.

case-50.title: Generate a ski hut scene in one pass
case-50.takeaway: DesignArena asked Neon and Argon to generate the same Alpine hut setting and published the side-by-side outputs.
case-50.notes: DesignArena preferred elements of both renderings. It reports that Neon added snowfall without being asked.
case-50.action: Check the hut, snow, and trees separately when assessing this one-pass scene comparison.

case-51.title: Render a voxel fantasy castle
case-51.takeaway: The creator shares a voxel castle produced at Neon xhigh.
case-51.notes: The creator reports one prompt and a 27-minute completion time.
case-51.action: Review the final scene and the reported run time when evaluating a one-prompt build.

case-52.title: Compare an octopus cycling animation with Astra
case-52.takeaway: The tester recorded Astra xhigh at 21 minutes 53 seconds and USD 2.52, and Neon high at 41 minutes and USD 4.02.
case-52.notes: The author calls the animation quality close. This is one run at different reasoning settings.
case-52.action: Compare the animation and cost while keeping the two reasoning settings explicit.

case-53.title: Three.js butterfly animation
case-53.takeaway: A creator used Neon xhigh in Antigravity to build a Three.js butterfly animation.
case-53.notes: The creator reported 57 minutes, about 23% of their five-hour quota, and 7% of their weekly quota.
case-53.action: Use the clip and its reported resource use to size a similar Three.js experiment.

case-54.title: Build components and motion from reference images
case-54.takeaway: The creator used visual references to generate several components and accompanying motion.
case-54.notes: The demo shows the result. The claim about how it feels compared with Opus is the creator's judgment.
case-54.action: Supply visual references and evaluate layout fidelity and motion as separate criteria.

case-55.title: Pixel wizard world in Three.js
case-55.takeaway: A creator gave Neon reference images and refined the Three.js scene over three passes.
case-55.notes: The creator reported using 39% of their five-hour quota and 11% of their weekly quota in Antigravity.
case-55.action: Use the three passes to judge how visual polish changes with iteration.

case-56.title: Castle rendering benchmark
case-56.takeaway: The creator used Neon for a castle benchmark and posted video and stills.
case-56.notes: The creator reported using about 4% of a weekly quota on their plan. The post does not establish whether that usage generalizes to other accounts.
case-56.action: Treat the castle as one creator's visual benchmark and retain account-specific quota context.

case-57.title: Recreate Alan Turing's 1936 study
case-57.takeaway: Google used Neon with Antigravity Swarm to build an interactive reconstruction from archival photos.
case-57.notes: The scene includes King's Chapel, Turing's study and a working simulation of a universal Turing machine on the desk.
case-57.action: Check archival fidelity and interactive functionality as separate parts of the reconstruction.

case-58.title: Build a side-scrolling obstacle game
case-58.takeaway: The tester asked Neon for a Flappy Bird-style prototype and posted a recording.
case-58.notes: The author reports about five minutes and discusses their own impressions of cost and usage.
case-58.action: Test the obstacle loop and collision behavior when you review a small game prototype.

case-59.title: Compare sword and shield combat scenes
case-59.takeaway: The tester posted a video with labeled Fable 5.2 and Neon outputs for a combat game scene.
case-59.notes: The video records two results and does not establish a general model ranking.
case-59.action: Use the two labeled clips to assess the visual and interaction differences yourself.

case-60.title: Build a synthwave mini-golf game
case-60.takeaway: Google Antigravity shows Gemini 4 Neon using Swarm to build a 3D mini-golf game from one prompt.
case-60.notes: The footage shows eight worker agents, a browser playthrough and the built-in verifier checking all eight courses.
case-60.action: Watch how the worker agents divide the work and how the browser verifies the eight courses.

case-61.title: Compare animated knight duels
case-61.takeaway: The tester posted separate labeled Opus 5.5 and Neon outputs for a duel between armored characters.
case-61.notes: The post asks readers to judge the rendered results and does not disclose a controlled protocol.
case-61.action: Compare motion readability and character staging in the two duel clips.

case-62.title: Make an expressionist art game in one HTML file
case-62.takeaway: The developer used Neon to create an endless JavaScript art game contained in one HTML file.
case-62.notes: The developer published the result and describes its expressionist visual treatment.
case-62.action: Inspect the visual style and controls of a game delivered as one HTML file.

case-63.title: Compare ice-boss game prototypes
case-63.takeaway: The tester posted labeled Neon and Opus 5.5 outputs for a first-person ice-boss encounter.
case-63.notes: The video provides a visual comparison. The post leaves the prompt, settings, timing, and winner open.
case-63.action: Use the labeled encounter footage to judge scene readability without assuming a shared prompt.

case-64.title: Watermelon basketball demo
case-64.takeaway: The tester shares a Neon watermelon basketball video.
case-64.notes: The author names the tested model and links the result but provides no timings or build settings.
case-64.action: Review the arena, movement, and ball interaction in this prototype.

case-65.title: Build a gaussian splatting bakery platformer
case-65.takeaway: The creator used Neon to turn a C++20 and WebGPU gaussian splatting engine into a four-tower platformer.
case-65.notes: The creator reported three prompts and about 60 minutes of active swarm time, then asked the model to record the demo.
case-65.action: Use the recorded playthrough to distinguish rendering work from gameplay tuning.

case-66.title: Build a 3D game with Antigravity Swarm
case-66.takeaway: The developer used Neon and Antigravity Swarm to build a small 3D game.
case-66.notes: The developer describes support for both mobile and desktop and shares a walkthrough thread.
case-66.action: Review the resulting mobile and desktop paths separately in a Swarm-assisted build.

case-67.title: Space racing prototype
case-67.takeaway: A creator reported building a space racer with Neon at high reasoning.
case-67.notes: The creator reported a run of about 15 minutes costing USD 1.50 and posted the output.
case-67.action: Compare the playable result with the reported time and cost of the first build.

case-68.title: Tower defense prototype
case-68.takeaway: A developer posted gameplay from a Neon-built tower defense prototype.
case-68.notes: The developer reported about 20 minutes and 2% of their five-hour quota. The smooth-play claim is the developer's assessment.
case-68.action: Test the tower defense loop yourself before generalizing from the author's smoothness report.

case-69.title: Build a first-person ski simulator
case-69.takeaway: Google reports using Neon to create a WebGL2 freeride simulator on Mont Blanc and Chamonix terrain.
case-69.notes: The demonstration includes six ski lines, a 120 Hz physics loop, track carving and spatial audio.
case-69.action: Look at terrain, movement, and audio separately when evaluating the ski simulator.

case-70.title: Summarize model choices in a research table
case-70.takeaway: The author attributes a Gemini 4 model selection table to research performed by Neon.
case-70.notes: The screenshot is the resulting recommendation. Its entries are the output of the research task, not independently verified product guidance.
case-70.action: Verify the claims in a model-selection table against the sources before using it to decide.

case-71.title: Co-create a launch film with Neon
case-71.takeaway: A Google team member reports co-creating a film with Neon and shares the result.
case-71.notes: The film is a provider-side demonstration. The post does not identify which tools rendered individual frames or audio.
case-71.action: Use the film as a provider example and identify the other tools before attributing production steps.

case-72.title: Explain equipment mechanics in a VR game
case-72.takeaway: The author used Neon to summarize equipment in the Meta Quest game H3VR2 and attached an illustrated explainer.
case-72.notes: The artifact documents the game scenario. The source does not identify the exact prompt or assign the video production to Neon.
case-72.action: Check the explanatory artifact against the game mechanics before treating it as a guide.

case-73.title: Inspect a self-assessment during image cropping
case-73.takeaway: The tester reports that Neon complimented its own crop during an image editing test.
case-73.notes: The screenshot documents a single interaction. It does not establish crop quality or the behavior of other tools.
case-73.action: Judge the crop itself before relying on the model's description of its quality.

case-74.title: Turn an article into editable slides
case-74.takeaway: The creator sent Neon an article and used a public slide-making skill.
case-74.notes: The creator reports that the workflow generated and inserted images and delivered editable Google Slides. The post describes the overall workflow without identifying the image generator.
case-74.action: Check that the slides are editable and that their images support the original article.

case-75.title: Generate a fantasy novel opening
case-75.takeaway: The author used Neon for a writing test and published the opening of a Chinese fantasy story.
case-75.notes: The post shows a completed opening excerpt. Its length and quality do not establish the model's long-form performance.
case-75.action: Review the opening for style and voice before drawing conclusions about a longer draft.

case-76.title: Interpret an original Dario joke
case-76.takeaway: The author reports that Neon understood a joke they wrote while Opus 5.5 did not.
case-76.notes: This is one attempt with screenshots. It does not establish broad writing or reasoning performance.
case-76.action: Use matched examples to separate understanding a specific joke from broad writing ability.

case-77.title: Build a computer-vision lab in Sheets
case-77.takeaway: Google reports that a Neon swarm turned one reference image into a 100,000-cell spreadsheet.
case-77.notes: The demo uses more than 500,000 formulas across six modes for tasks including edge detection, depth mapping and relighting.
case-77.action: Inspect which effects come from formulas when evaluating a spreadsheet-only visualization.

case-78.title: Measure domain performance on the Vals Index
case-78.takeaway: Vals AI reports 70.9% for Neon and a second-place aggregate rank, 0.4 points behind Fable 5.2.
case-78.notes: The evaluator also reports first place on its Finance and Legal indexes and Tax Agent and Legal Research tasks.
case-78.action: Use task-level results to see whether the aggregate rank matches your domain.

case-79.title: Test interactive demos during early access
case-79.takeaway: The author reports using Neon in Antigravity to build 17 interactive demos and documented additional coding and tool tests.
case-79.notes: The published thread reports both successes and issues. Its demos are grouped as one early-access test series.
case-79.action: Compare the successful prototypes with the failures reported in the same early-access thread.

case-80.title: Compare agent sessions in Agent Arena
case-80.takeaway: Arena reports Neon High at 1336 points, ranked second, with a USD 2.82 median cost per task.
case-80.notes: Arena's post describes an evaluation based on 4.2 thousand community agent sessions.
case-80.action: Use median per-task cost alongside the reported score when comparing Agent Arena results.

case-81.title: Place Neon in Text Arena
case-81.takeaway: Arena reports Neon High at 1518, behind Carbon High at 1526 and Argon High at 1521.
case-81.notes: This is a Text Arena snapshot from the benchmark publisher.
case-81.action: Compare the same Arena snapshot and reasoning settings when reading the scores.

case-82.title: Rank printable 3D figures in Wojak-Bench
case-82.takeaway: The benchmark coauthor reported that Neon debuted in fourth place. The posted leaderboard snapshot gives Neon a rating of 1056.
case-82.notes: Models turn the same reference drawing into printable figures. Visitors compare pairs of outputs, so the live rating can change as votes accumulate.
case-82.action: Read the posted placement as a snapshot of the pairwise comparison, and check the current board before citing a rating.

case-83.title: Compare coding agents with their harnesses
